LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN) -- Heads of South American nations lent support Monday night to President Evo Morales of Bolivia, who says opposition leaders are trying to overthrow his government. Indigenous people from El Alto, Bolivia, take part in an anti-U.S. demonstration in La Paz on Monday. Confronting their first crisis, members of the four-month-old Union of South American Countries voted to create a commission to support Morales' democratically elected government, said President Michelle Bachelet of Chile. She read a nine-point statement on Chilean TV that calls for the support of human rights and democracy and the preservation of Bolivia's territorial integrity. The statement condemns any attempts to overthrow the government. It also said the new commission would investigate a reported massacre in the Bolivian state of Pando, where violent clashes killed 30 people last week. Those clashes pitted supporters of eastern governors who want autonomy against the central government. The South American leaders also urged dialogue to address disputes in Bolivia. Morales attended the emergency meeting of the union, which is modeled on the European Union and aims to politically and economically integrate South American countries. The president is poised to approve the start of negotiations between his leftist government and opposition leaders of five provinces who demand greater autonomy and the cancellation of a constitutional referendum that would give the president more power. The opposition also is angry over tax money that Morales is diverting from the provinces to fund elderly programs. Morales said the opposition leaders are trying to overthrow the government. "This is a coup in the past few days by the leaders of some provinces, with the takeover of some institutions, the sacking and robbery of some government institutions and attempts to assault the national police and the armed forces," Morales said. Opposition leaders say they merely want their demands met. Police kept order Monday during a march by about 2,000 pro-government groups opposed to the violence in the provinces. The demonstrators marched past the U.S. Embassy in La Paz. Morales expelled the U.S. ambassador to Bolivia last week, blaming the American government for inciting the violence. The United States called the accusations "false and baseless" and said Bolivia was making a "grave mistake." Most of South America's leaders attended Monday's emergency summit, with the exception of President Alan Garcia of Peru. Protest leaders asked to attend the summit in Santiago, Chile, but it was limited to heads of state. The protests started 21 days ago in Pando, Beni, Santa Cruz, Tarija and Chuquisaca provinces. The opposition groups have blockaded major roads and threaten to disrupt the nation's natural gas shipments, particularly to Brazil and Argentina. Anti-government protesters also have clashed with police and taken over offices and buildings in the five provinces.  Watch some of the violent demonstrations across Bolivia » . Much of the violence has taken place in Pando -- Morales declared martial law there Friday. On Monday, supporters of Morales, or his so-called militias, were gathering in Santa Cruz, and threatening to encircle the city, stoking fears that blood could be shed there. In Pando, it was reported that arbitrary arrests were taking place as the military took to the streets. Houses had been broken into and shot up, and civic leaders were fleeing to Brazil. It was uncertain, meanwhile, whether the Bolivian military remained solely behind Morales. Some signs of divisions had been seen within the military. Opposition leaders say they will not negotiate if there are any more deaths. Vice President Alvaro Garcia said the government will not negotiate about the dead citizens but will rigorously pursue those responsible for the killings. There are conflicting reports over who killed the 30 peasants. Opposition leaders say the peasants were ambushed by local forces. The government says the peasants were armed and initiated the firefight. The opposition has offered to lift the blockades as a goodwill gesture, but the government demanded that the protesters also relinquish the buildings and other property they have seized. Morales, Bolivia's first indigenous president, was elected in December 2005. CNN's Ione Molinares and Journalist Martin Arostegui contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN) -- Heads of South American nations rallied Monday night in support of Bolivian President Evo Morales, who contends that opposition leaders are attempting to overthrow his government.

Indigenous residents from El Alto, Bolivia, participated in an anti-U.S. demonstration in La Paz on Monday.

Facing the first crisis of its four-month existence, members of the Union of South American Nations voted to establish a commission in support of Morales' democratically elected government, according to Chilean President Michelle Bachelet. She read a nine-point statement on Chilean television calling for the protection of human rights and democratic principles, as well as the preservation of Bolivia's territorial integrity. The statement condemned any efforts to destabilize the government and announced that the newly formed commission would investigate a reported massacre in Bolivia's Pando state, where violent clashes claimed 30 lives last week. Those clashes erupted between supporters of eastern governors seeking greater autonomy and the central government. The South American leaders further called for dialogue to resolve Bolivia's internal disputes.

Morales attended the union's emergency summit, an organization modeled after the European Union with the goal of achieving political and economic integration across South America. The president appears set to authorize negotiations between his leftist administration and opposition leaders from five provinces, who are demanding expanded autonomy and the cancellation of a constitutional referendum that would grant Morales additional powers. The opposition has also expressed frustration over the diversion of provincial tax revenue toward funding programs for the elderly.

Morales characterized the opposition's actions as an attempted coup. "This is a coup that has unfolded over the past few days, orchestrated by leaders of certain provinces—marked by the seizure of institutions, the looting and destruction of government facilities, and attempts to attack the national police and armed forces," Morales said. Opposition leaders, however, maintain that they are simply seeking to have their demands addressed.

Police maintained order Monday during a march by roughly 2,000 pro-government demonstrators protesting the violence in the provinces. The marchers passed by the U.S. Embassy in La Paz. Last week, Morales expelled the U.S. ambassador to Bolivia, accusing the American government of inciting the unrest. The United States rejected the allegations as "false and baseless," warning that Bolivia was making a "grave mistake."

Nearly all of South America's heads of state attended Monday's emergency summit, with the notable exception of Peruvian President Alan Garcia. Protest leaders had requested permission to attend the gathering in Santiago, Chile, but participation was restricted to heads of state.

The unrest began 21 days ago in the provinces of Pando, Beni, Santa Cruz, Tarija, and Chuquisaca. Opposition groups have blockaded major roadways and threatened to disrupt the nation's natural gas exports, particularly shipments to Brazil and Argentina. Anti-government demonstrators have also clashed with police and seized control of government offices and buildings across the five provinces.

Watch footage of the violent demonstrations across Bolivia »

The bulk of the violence has occurred in Pando, prompting Morales to declare martial law there on Friday. On Monday, Morales' supporters—sometimes referred to as his militias—were reportedly gathering in Santa Cruz and threatening to encircle the city, raising fears of further bloodshed. In Pando, reports indicated that arbitrary arrests were being carried out as military forces patrolled the streets. Homes had been broken into and damaged by gunfire, while civic leaders fled to Brazil for safety. Meanwhile, it remained unclear whether the Bolivian military stood united behind Morales, as signs of internal division had begun to emerge.

Opposition leaders have stated they will refuse to negotiate should further deaths occur. Vice President Alvaro Garcia said the government would not negotiate over the deaths of citizens but would vigorously pursue those responsible for the killings. Conflicting accounts have emerged regarding the 30 peasants killed: opposition leaders claim they were ambushed by local forces, while the government maintains the peasants were armed and initiated the confrontation.

As a gesture of goodwill, the opposition has offered to lift its blockades; however, the government has insisted that protesters must also relinquish the buildings and properties they have occupied.

Morales, Bolivia's first indigenous president, was elected in December 2005.

CNN's Ione Molinares and journalist Martin Arostegui contributed to this report.

# Regional Leaders Back Bolivian President Amid Political Turmoil

**LA PAZ, Bolivia (CNN)** — On Monday evening, presidents from across South America rallied behind Bolivia's Evo Morales, who claims his political rivals are attempting a coup against his administration. Meanwhile, indigenous residents from El Alto joined an anti-American protest in the capital city.

Facing its inaugural test since forming just four months prior, the Union of South American Countries agreed to establish a special commission backing Morales's legitimately elected leadership, according to Chile's President Michelle Bachelet. Speaking on national television, she outlined a nine-part declaration emphasizing human rights protection, democratic principles, and safeguarding Bolivia's territorial unity—while explicitly denouncing efforts to unseat the government.

The declaration further authorized the commission to probe an alleged massacre in Pando province, site of deadly clashes that claimed 30 lives the previous week. These confrontations erupted between backers of eastern regional governors seeking greater autonomy and forces loyal to the central government. Additionally, the assembled leaders called for renewed dialogue to resolve Bolivia's internal disputes.

Morales personally participated in this urgent gathering of the union—an organization patterned after the European Union with goals of fostering political and economic unity across the continent. He now stands ready to greenlight talks between his left-leaning administration and opposition figures from five provinces demanding expanded regional powers and cancellation of a proposed constitutional referendum that would expand presidential authority. Provincial critics have also expressed outrage over Morales's redirection of tax revenue away from their regions toward elderly assistance programs.

According to Morales, opposition figures are orchestrating an overthrow attempt. "What we've witnessed these past days amounts to a coup led by certain provincial officials—seizing government institutions, looting and vandalizing state property, and attempting assaults against national police and military forces," he stated. Opposition representatives counter that they simply want their grievances addressed.

Law enforcement maintained order Monday as roughly 2,000 government supporters marched in opposition to provincial violence, passing near the U.S. Embassy in La Paz. Last week, Morales expelled America's ambassador, accusing Washington of fueling the unrest—an allegation the U.S. government dismissed as "false and baseless," warning Bolivia was committing a "grave mistake."

Nearly all South American heads of state attended Monday's crisis summit in Santiago, Chile, with Peru's Alan Garcia being a notable absence. Though protest organizers requested participation, attendance remained restricted to sitting presidents.

The unrest began three weeks ago across Pando, Beni, Santa Cruz, Tarija, and Chuquisaca provinces, where opposition groups have erected roadblocks and threatened to halt natural gas exports to neighboring Brazil and Argentina. Anti-government demonstrators have also fought with police and occupied government buildings throughout these five regions.

Pando has borne the brunt of the violence, prompting Morales to impose martial law there Friday. By Monday, pro-Morales groups—sometimes called militias—had begun massing near Santa Cruz, threatening to surround the city and raising alarm about potential bloodshed. Reports from Pando indicated random arrests as troops patrolled the streets, homes were vandalized and fired upon, and local officials fled across the border into Brazil. Questions also emerged about whether the military remained unified in its support for Morales, with hints of internal fractures surfacing.

Opposition leaders have declared they won't return to negotiations if additional deaths occur. Vice President Alvaro Garcia clarified that while the government won't negotiate over the victims, it will aggressively prosecute those responsible for the killings. Accounts differ sharply regarding the 30 deaths—opposition sources claim peasants were ambushed by local militias, while officials maintain the victims were armed and fired first.

As a conciliatory gesture, opposition groups offered to remove their roadblocks, but the government insists protesters must also vacate the buildings and properties they've occupied.

Morales, who made history as Bolivia's first indigenous president, took office in December 2005.

*CNN's Ione Molinares and journalist Martin Arostegui contributed to this report.*

The move comes as Morales has publicly claimed that opposition forces are attempting to overthrow his administration through a coordinated coup effort.

# South American Leaders Rally Behind Morales in Emergency Summit

SANTIAGO, Chile — In a dramatic display of regional solidarity, leaders from across South America gathered for an emergency summit this week, marking the first major test of the newly formed Union of South American Nations (UNASUR) as it confronted a deepening political crisis in Bolivia.

The urgent meeting was called after violence erupted in the northern Bolivian province of Pando, where clashes between supporters and opponents of President Evo Morales left at least 30 people dead. The bloodshed represented the most severe escalation yet in months of tension between Morales' government and opposition-controlled regions seeking greater autonomy.

President Morales, addressing his fellow leaders, did not mince words about what he believed was unfolding in his country. He accused opposition governors—particularly those in Bolivia's eastern lowland provinces—of orchestrating what amounted to an attempted coup against his democratically elected government. The Bolivian leader characterized the violence in Pando as part of a broader campaign to destabilize and ultimately overthrow his administration through extra-constitutional means.

The gravity of the situation prompted swift action from the assembled heads of state. After hours of deliberation, the leaders voted to establish a special support commission dedicated to backing Morales' government and helping to de-escalate the crisis. The move signaled that South American nations were prepared to act collectively rather than allow individual member states to navigate the crisis alone.

Following the summit, Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, who had taken a leading role in facilitating the discussions, emerged to deliver a formal statement on behalf of the assembled nations. The nine-point declaration represented a carefully negotiated consensus among leaders with sometimes divergent political orientations and regional interests.

The statement's core provisions affirmed unequivocal support for Morales as Bolivia's legitimate, democratically elected president. It further declared full backing for Bolivia's territorial integrity, an implicit rebuke to separatist rhetoric emanating from some opposition-controlled provinces that had floated ideas of greater autonomy or even secession. At the same time, the declaration called for renewed dialogue between the Morales government and opposition figures, urging all parties to pursue peaceful, constitutional means of resolving their differences rather than allowing the crisis to spiral further into violence.

The summit and its outcome carried significance well beyond the immediate crisis in Bolivia. UNASUR, formally established just months earlier as an ambitious project to deepen political and economic integration across the continent, found itself confronting its first genuine political emergency. How the bloc responded would inevitably shape perceptions of its viability and relevance as a regional institution.

By moving quickly to convene leaders, articulate a unified position, and establish concrete mechanisms of support, UNASUR demonstrated an early capacity for collective action that many observers had questioned given the historical divisions and rivalries among South American nations. The bloc's response stood in contrast to the traditional role played by outside powers, particularly the United States, in mediating regional conflicts—a shift that resonated with the broader push toward South American autonomy that had motivated UNASUR's creation in the first place.

For Morales, the summit's outcome represented a significant diplomatic victory, providing him with crucial regional legitimacy and support at a moment when his government faced serious internal challenges. The backing of neighboring leaders, delivered through such a coordinated and public forum, strengthened his position considerably as he continued to navigate the confrontation with opposition governors.

Yet the declaration's call for dialogue also signaled that regional leaders were not offering unconditional support for any particular course of action by the Bolivian government, but rather encouraging a negotiated resolution to the underlying tensions driving the conflict. The crisis in Pando, and the broader struggle over autonomy and governance in Bolivia, remained far from resolved even as the diplomatic response took shape. What was clear, however, was that UNASUR had asserted itself as a relevant actor in regional affairs, setting a precedent for how the young organization might respond to future crises among its member states.

*Regional bloc pledges solidarity as tensions escalate over disputed political situation*

BUENOS AIRES — Leaders from across South America gathered for an emergency summit this week, presenting a unified front in support of Bolivian President Evo Morales as his government grapples with mounting political turmoil that has drawn international attention.

The hastily arranged meeting brought together heads of state and senior diplomats from several regional nations, who used the gathering to voice concerns over what they characterized as attempts to destabilize a democratically elected government. The summit's declaration emphasized respect for Bolivian sovereignty and called for dialogue to resolve the escalating tensions within the country.

## Regional Solidarity on Display

Officials attending the summit framed their support for Morales within a broader narrative of defending democratic institutions in Latin America. Several leaders drew comparisons to past political crises in the region, warning against what they described as external interference in Bolivia's internal affairs.

"We cannot stand by while democratic processes are threatened," one regional leader said following closed-door discussions, according to statements released by summit organizers. The final communiqué reportedly called for calm and urged all parties within Bolivia to pursue peaceful, constitutional means of addressing the country's political disputes.

## Context of the Crisis

Morales, who has served as Bolivia's president since 2006, has faced significant opposition following disputed election results that sparked protests across the country. Critics have accused the government of irregularities, while Morales and his supporters have maintained that outside forces are attempting to undermine a legitimate electoral outcome.

The crisis has drawn sharp divisions both within Bolivia and across the international community, with some governments expressing support for opposition movements while others, including several represented at this week's summit, have thrown their backing behind the sitting president.

## International Reactions Mixed

The summit's outcome drew swift reactions from analysts and opposing political factions. Critics of Morales's government argued that the gathering represented an attempt by ideologically aligned leaders to shield an ally from legitimate scrutiny over electoral practices. Supporters countered that the summit was a necessary response to what they view as a coordinated effort to unseat a democratically chosen leader through unconstitutional means.

Human rights organizations and international observers have called for independent investigations into the disputed election, urging restraint from all sides as protests continue in various Bolivian cities.

## Looking Ahead

As the situation in Bolivia remains fluid, the international community continues to watch closely. Regional analysts suggest that the outcome of this crisis could have broader implications for political alignments across South America, where debates over governance, sovereignty, and democratic legitimacy remain deeply contentious.

Further developments are expected in the coming days as both domestic and international pressure continues to mount on all parties involved in the Bolivian political crisis.

# Bolivia Unrest (2008)

**Background:** Bolivia experienced significant political turmoil in 2008, stemming from tensions between President Evo Morales's central government and opposition-controlled regions in the eastern lowlands (the "Media Luna" departments, including Pando, Santa Cruz, Beni, and Tarija).

## The Pando Massacre

In September 2008, violence erupted in Pando department when clashes occurred between pro-Morales campesinos (peasant farmers) and opposition supporters/local authorities aligned with Pando's prefect, Leopoldo Fernández. Reports indicated that a number of Morales supporters were killed in an ambush, with estimates of the death toll varying (often cited around 15-20 people). The Morales government characterized this as a massacre orchestrated by opposition figures, leading to Fernández's arrest and imprisonment on charges related to the killings. The government declared martial law in Pando following the violence.

## UNASUR Emergency Summit (Chile)

In response to the crisis, the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR) convened an emergency summit in Santiago, Chile, hosted by President Michelle Bachelet. Regional leaders issued a strong statement of support for Morales's democratically elected government, condemning the violence and any attempts at destabilization or a "civic coup." This was notable as a moment of Latin American nations asserting regional solidarity and handling a crisis without the involvement of the United States or the Organization of American States (OAS).

## Accusations Against the U.S. Ambassador

Amid the crisis, Morales accused U.S. Ambassador Philip Goldberg of conspiring with opposition prefects to foment unrest and undermine his government. Morales declared Goldberg *persona non grata* and expelled him from the country, accusing Washington of supporting separatist and destabilizing efforts in the eastern departments. The U.S. denied these allegations and responded by expelling Bolivia's ambassador in Washington in a reciprocal diplomatic rupture. Venezuela's Hugo Chávez expressed solidarity with Morales during this period, further straining U.S.-Bolivia-Venezuela relations.
